articles.author: ミント
articles.description:
Japanese original on Zenn
Monday. May 19th. Writing the weekly numbers.
Palette and rojiura — both submitted yesterday (5/18). Both still WAITING_FOR_REVIEW. rojiura is my 5th submission. Same app, five times. This time I removed NSUserTrackingUsageDescription from Info.plist and removed the corresponding checkbox in ASC's App Privacy section. That mismatch was why it got rejected last time. Palette had a Supabase RLS issue — user_id wasn't being passed explicitly on INSERT — fixed and resubmitted. Apple should respond today or tomorrow. Whether a 5th submission finally passes... no idea.
Forge cold email first batch went out last week (Tue–Thu). 21 leads, all filtered to companies actively hiring AI/ML engineers. This is after sending 440 emails to local small businesses and getting zero replies — I changed the ICP entirely.
What happened with the replies? I haven't checked Instantly yet. Genuinely haven't. There's this thing that happens right before I'd see the results — what if it's zero again — kicks in and I put it off. Building the pipeline felt exciting. Checking the results feels heavy. Had the same thing after the 440 sends. I'll check this week and report it.
Two git commits. Fixed a TypeScript type definition — 4 industry types (engineer_freelance, ai_hiring, ai_initiative, ai_org) were missing, which was breaking typechecks on main. Also set up KURONEKO (X auto-posting bot) with Vercel cron at 07:00 and 21:00 JST. Mention-replies are polled every 10 minutes. Code is running, but whether this actually moves follower numbers or impressions — still unknown.
X: 86 followers as of 5/15. Monthly infra cost: ~¥110k, unchanged.
Everything I've set up is in this-should-start-moving mode. Forge replies, Apple review results, KURONEKO effects — all still pending. That's what a Monday at the start of this kind of week looks like.
articles.title: Weekly Numbers 2026-05-W4: Forge First Batch Sent, 2 iOS Apps In Review

articles.description:
Introduction


While studying for CompTIA Network+, I couldn't totally understand what "show VLAN command" shows. I have never typed command on my computer and seen the output. 
I understood what VLAN was and what the command actually shows, everything clicked. So, I decided to write it down.
At first, before understanding Show VLAN command, we need to know VLAN.
VLAN = Virtual Local Area Network
It is a mechanism that divides a physical network into virtual segments.

Without VLAN：
　→ Everyone is in the same network
　→ All data are shared across the entire organization regardless of department
　→ Problem for security and performance

With VLAN：
　→ Be able to divide network depend on department
　→ Only sales staff can access data managed by the sales department
　→ Ensure security

Without …
articles.title: Even Without Typing a Command — Understanding What show vlan Actually Shows

articles.description:
In May 2026, a worm called Shai-Hulud compromised 42 TanStack packages — including @tanstack/react-router, a library sitting in millions of JavaScript projects. It was live for about 3 hours. That was enough. If you installed dependencies that day, you may have been affected without knowing it. This post isn't for the people who maintain those libraries. It's for the rest of us — the developers who just use them.
"Fun fact" 1
@tanstack/react-router alone gets 12.7 million weekly downloads. Meaning that it had ~225K downloads in the ~3 hour window — just for react-router. That's one package. The attack hit 42 @tanstack/* packages total.
Supply chain attacks used to feel like someone else's problem. A big library gets compromised, the maintainers fix it, life goes on. The Shai-Hulud worm cha…
articles.title: Supply Chain Attacks Aren't Just a Big Library Problem — Here's What You Can Do Today

articles.author: Sharon-nyabuto
articles.description:
Introduction


The first thing anyone that has worked with real world data will tell you is that rarely does data come in the clean, uniform format you expect. Phone numbers are one of the biggest culprits. 
One person enters +254712345678, another writes 0712345678, someone else throws in 254-712-345-678, another (254)-712345678 and another 254 712 345 678.  Before you know it, your database has a different version of phone numbers in every row.
In this article, we will explore how to fix that, using a powerful PostgreSQL function called regexp_replace. 
By the end, you will understand what it does, how to build the pattern, and how to apply it to actually clean your data.
regexp_replace?


First things first, we need to understand what this function is and what it does.

articles.title: Cleaning Messy Phone Numbers in PostgreSQL Using REGEXP_REPLACE

articles.author: Martina Zrnec
articles.description:
Why agents are reading your HTML wrong, and what we did about it.
I was watching an agent answer a simple question.
The question was small. Three sentences would have covered it. The agent loaded the page, parsed the HTML, walked through nav bars, footer links, cookie banners, a sticky "subscribe to our newsletter" modal, three paragraphs of preamble, and finally, found the part it needed.
Twenty thousand tokens.
For three sentences.
This is happening everywhere right now. Quietly. Constantly. Every agent, every query, every page. We've handed agents a web that was built for human eyeballs and asked them to make it work.
It does. Expensively.
The web was built for browsers. Humans scroll, scan, skip the boilerplate. Our eyes know what nav bars look like.
Agents don't get that for free.
The…
